title: Proposal of a consistent value for the mean excitation energy of liquid water using advanced modeling, detailed simulations and precission proton Bragg curves
authors: Pablo de Vera, Isabel Abril, Flávio Matias, Julian M. B. Shorto, Hélio Yoriyaz, Rafael Garcia-Molina
abstract: Protontherapy precision depends on accurately knowing the stopping power of liquid water, as it is the most abundant component of soft body tissues. Difficulties when working with volatile liquids have led to a long-standing debate regarding the values of the stopping power and the mean excitation energy $I$ of liquid water. The equivalence between the stopping power of liquid water and amorphous ice per unit mass density across all clinically relevant proton energies opens the possibility to obtain a reliable estimation of the $I$-value of liquid water. In this work, we employ two complementary theoretical methodologies to assess the proton stopping power of water. The MELF-GOS (Mermin Energy Loss Function - Generalized Oscillator Strengths) approach, based on the perturbative dielectric formalism, serves as an accurate reference for sufficiently high energies, while the novel non-perturbative TDDFT-Penn (time-dependent density functional theory - Penn) method ensures accuracy for energies even below the stopping maximum. These stopping-power values were incorporated into the simulation code SEICS (Simulation of Energetic Ions and Clusters through Solids) to evaluate proton Bragg curves from $1$ to $230$ MeV. Comparisons with available precise depth-dose measurements provide critical insights that help establish the consistent value $I = 79.4$ eV for liquid water, providing robust physical grounds for improving range prediction for treatment planning.
summary: This paper tackles the critical problem of determining the mean excitation energy ($I$) for liquid water, essential for accurate proton therapy dose planning. The authors use a combination of advanced theoretical modeling (MELF-GOS, TDDFT-Penn) and detailed simulations to calculate stopping power across wide energy ranges. They conclude that $I = 79.4 	ext{ eV}$ provides the most consistent value matching both theory and experimental Bragg curve measurements.
main_problem: The primary goal is establishing a consistent, reliable value for the mean excitation energy ($I$) of liquid water, which is critical for accurately predicting proton stopping power in medical physics applications like protontherapy.
main_result: By combining advanced theoretical models (MELF-GOS and TDDFT-Penn) with detailed simulations of proton Bragg curves, the authors converge on a consistent value of $I = 79.4 	ext{ eV}$ for liquid water.
method: The study employs complementary theoretical methods—the perturbative MELF-GOS approach and the non-perturbative TDDFT-Penn method—to calculate stopping power ($dE/dx$) across various proton energies, which are then used in SEICS simulations to generate Bragg curves.
model_or_system: The physical system is liquid water ($	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$), treated as the primary medium for high-energy proton beams. The analysis relies on dielectric formalism and time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) to model energy loss mechanisms.
key_observables: Stopping power ($dE/dx$), Mean Excitation Energy ($I$), and simulated/measured Proton Bragg curves (depth-dose profiles).
important_parameters: Proton beam energies ranging from $1$ to $230 	ext{ MeV}$; the derived value of $I = 79.4 	ext{ eV}$.
main_assumptions: The theoretical models assume that the stopping power can be accurately calculated using dielectric response functions, although limitations exist for very low energies where perturbative methods fail.
figures_summary: Figures compare simulated mass stopping power (MELF-GOS vs. TDDFT-Penn) against experimental data for liquid water and amorphous ice; another figure analyzes the Figure of Merit ($	ext{FoM}$) across various assumed $I$-values, highlighting $79.4 	ext{ eV}$ as optimal.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the necessity of accurate stopping power due to protontherapy needs, then detailing two complementary theoretical calculation methods (MELF-GOS and TDDFT-Penn), followed by applying these calculations to simulate Bragg curves, and finally using a Figure of Merit analysis on experimental data to confirm $I=79.4 	ext{ eV}$.
why_interesting: While the core physics is in condensed matter/radiation dosimetry, the reliance on advanced quantum mechanical methods like TDDFT and dielectric formalism for calculating energy loss functions connects conceptually to open quantum systems theory and response functions.
